learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Hashing and Integrity.

content.intro: This lesson covers hashing and integrity in the Cryptography and Secure Communications track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Use vetted platform libraries and current standards; never invent an encryption scheme or treat encoding as encryption. The specific focus here is hashing and integrity; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A general-purpose cryptographic hash is useful for integrity checks but is too fast for password storage. Password verification requires a dedicated, salted password-hashing scheme with a work factor that can be adjusted over time.

items.title: Cryptographic Hash Functions
items.text: A cryptographic hash maps data to a fixed-length digest used for integrity checks and other purposes. Hashes are not encryption and do not by themselves authenticate an origin; password storage needs a dedicated password-hashing algorithm.

items.title: Collision Resistance and Preimage Resistance
items.text: For collision resistance and preimage resistance, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: File Integrity Verification
items.text: Integrity means data and system state remain accurate and protected against unauthorized or accidental change. Identify trusted sources, validation checks, and evidence that a change was expected.

items.title: Password Hashing with Dedicated Password-Hashing Algorithms

items.title: HMAC and Message Authentication
items.text: Authentication verifies a claimed identity; it does not decide all permissions. Use phishing-resistant factors where practical, protect recovery flows, rate-limit failures, and avoid reusing credentials.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
import hashlib

# Integrity demonstration for a synthetic string, not password storage.
artifact = b"CodeLeaf training artifact v1"
digest = hashlib.sha256(artifact).hexdigest()
print("algorithm: SHA-256")
print("digest length:", len(digest))
print("same input, same digest:", digest == hashlib.sha256(artifact).hexdigest())
content_blocks.expected_output:
algorithm: SHA-256
digest length: 64
same input, same digest: True
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Cryptography provides specific security properties only when algorithms, protocols, key handling, randomness, and implementation are all appropriate. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: A general-purpose cryptographic hash is useful for integrity checks but is too fast for password storage. Password verification requires a dedicated, salted password-hashing scheme with a work factor that can be adjusted over time. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Hashing and Integrity. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Cryptographic Hash Functions; SHA-2 and SHA-3 Families; Collision Resistance and Preimage Resistance), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Hashing and Integrity is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.
